claims.text: Overhand grip, slightly narrower than shoulder width; pull the bar straight up to about chin level, then lower with control.

quotes.text: Grip the bar with an overhand grip, slightly narrower than shoulder-width apart. Pull the bar straight up until it is at the level of your chin. With control, lower the bar back to the starting position.
quotes.where: How to Do Barbell Upright Row

claims.text: The upright row has a reputation for shoulder pain from impingement at the top; light weights, few sets at first and not raising the upper arms above shoulder height reduce the risk.

quotes.text: you can mitigate the risk of shoulder pain by starting with light weights and a low number of sets and by avoiding elevating your upper arms above shoulder height at the top of the movement.

claims.text: Keep the bar close to the body and the elbows directly out to the sides; lift with the shoulders and traps, not the arms or wrists.

quotes.text: Lift the barbell straight up, and keep it close to your body.
Make sure to keep the elbows directly out to the sides. Ensure to lift with your shoulders and traps, not your arms or wrists.

claims.text: Impingement usually comes from lifting the arm out to the side while it is rolled inward.

quotes.text: Generally, shoulder impingement occurs when you internally rotate the shoulder (roll the upper arm forward slightly) and then lift it out to the side.

claims.text: A too-narrow grip, rounded shoulders and pulling the bar up under the chin (elbows above the shoulders) all raise impingement risk.

quotes.text: If you pull the bar right up under your chin it’s no good. Lifting your elbows above your shoulders is another road to increase the likelihood of shoulder impingement.
If your hands are too narrowly placed your shoulders will be internally rotated as you raise the bar up.

claims.text: Safer version: hands about hip width, shoulder blades drawn back, bar only to the lower ribs with elbows at shoulder level.

quotes.text: Have your hands wide – at about hip-width. If your hands are wide there’s less chance of internal rotation. Draw the shoulder blades back and stabilize them as you lift the bar.
quotes.where: The right way to upright row

quotes.text: Limit how high you lift the bar. Only ever lift the bar to the lower ribs, with your elbows in line with shoulder level.
quotes.where: The right way to upright row

claims.text: Wider grips gave more deltoid and trapezius activity and less biceps activity in trained men.

quotes.text: The main findings of this investigation are increased deltoid and trapezius activity with increasing grip width, and correspondingly less BB activity. Therefore, those who seek to maximize involvement of the deltoid and trapezius muscles during the URR should use a wide grip.

claims.text: It mainly works the side delts, with front delts, trapezius and biceps secondary.

quotes.text: The barbell upright row is a shoulder exercise that primarily targets your lateral deltoids and secondary your front deltoids and trapezius.
quotes.where: Which Muscles Does the Barbell Upright Row Work?

claims.text: A cable upright row may feel easier on the shoulders than the barbell.

quotes.text: So if you feel like the barbell upright row might be a bit hard on your shoulder joints, you might want to give the cable version a go.

claims.text: Tempo: about 1-2 s up and 1-2 s down, controlled.

quotes.text: using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC).
With control, lower the bar back to the starting position.
quotes.where: How to Do Barbell Upright Row

claims.text: The upright row suits moderate reps and lighter weights, not heavy strength work; add load in small steps.

quotes.text: The upright is an isolation exercise that lends itself better to moderate rep ranges and lighter weights with a controlled movement in this case.
When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Stand with feet about shoulder width, upright, light core tension and chest up.

quotes.text: Make sure to stand about shoulder-width apart and keep an upright position. Keep a light tension in your core and chest up.

claims.text: The shoulder is one of the most common injury sites in resistance training (up to 36% of documented injuries).

quotes.text: The results of the review indicated that up to 36% of documented RT-related injuries and disorders occur at the shoulder complex.

claims.text: Wrap the thumbs around the bar.

quotes.text: Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar.

plate.viewWhy: Grip width and elbow height against the shoulders are side-to-side and up-down positions (c5, c6) that only the front view shows; the census draws it front.
plate.equipment: Straight barbell (cable is the other listed option, see variantLine), floor line.
plate.start: Standing upright, feet about shoulder width (c12), arms straight, bar at the thighs, overhand grip about shoulder width or a little wider (c6, c7).
plate.end: Elbows out to the sides and level with the shoulders, not above (c2, c6), bar close to the body at about the lower chest (c6, c3).

checkpoints.label: Elbows lead
checkpoints.what: Elbows go out to the sides and stay above the hands.

checkpoints.label: Shoulder height
checkpoints.what: Stop when the elbows reach shoulder level.

checkpoints.label: Bar close
checkpoints.what: The bar travels straight up close to the body.

mistake.what: Bar pulled up under the chin with the elbows above the shoulders.
mistake.why: Raising the elbows above the shoulders raises impingement risk (c5), and the top is where upright-row shoulder pain comes from (c2).

plate.variantLine: Barbell drawn. Cable version (low pulley, straight bar): all body and height claims (c2-c6, c12) hold; c9 says it may feel easier on the shoulders.

grip.width: About shoulder width or a little wider (hip width to wider); not close. Sources disagree: StrengthLog says slightly narrower than shoulders (c1), Les Mills and McAllister 2013 favour wider (c6, c7). The card takes the wider, lower-risk option.
grip.handContact: Bar across the base of the fingers (pull archetype).
grip.wrist: Straight; don't lift with the wrists.

setup.step: Stand upright, feet about shoulder width, chest up.
Overhand grip about hip width or a bit wider, thumbs around the bar.
Draw the shoulder blades back before the first pull.

posture.point: Elbows out to the sides, leading the bar.
Elbows no higher than the shoulders.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Pulling the bar up under the chin.
handlingMistakes.fix: Stop at the lower chest, elbows level with the shoulders.
Widen the grip to about hip width or more.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Lifting with the wrists and letting the elbows drop.
handlingMistakes.fix: Lead with the elbows out to the sides.

rows.means: Usually means the side delts are lifting.
Usually means the grip is narrow.

rows.where: Pinch at the top of the shoulder near the top of the lift
rows.means: Usually means impingement from lifting too high or too narrow.
rows.fix: Stop lower, widen the grip, go lighter.

risks.risk: Shoulder pinching at the top when the elbows rise above the shoulders.
The shoulder is a common injury site in weight training.

zooms.right: Overhand about hip width or wider, thumbs wrapped, wrists straight.
zooms.wrong: Hands touching in the middle, wrists curled up.

zooms.right: Elbows level with shoulders, bar at the lower chest.
zooms.wrong: Bar under the chin, elbows above the shoulders.

libraryDiff.why: Library primary side_delts, upper_traps and secondary biceps match (c7, c8). Add front_delts as secondary: StrengthLog names them (c8).
